title: The End Of The British Empire After World War 2
text:
The End Of The British Empire After World War 2

# The collapse of the British Empire 

 View video transcript Hide video transcript 

### Transcript

Voiceover: “At its peak in the 1920s, the British Empire controlled over one quarter of the earth's entire landmass. It was a dominant global force, a seemingly unstoppable empire that had existed for over three and a half centuries. And yet, within just a few decades, the British Empire would completely disintegrate."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "Colonialism is about ensuring the wealth and resources enrich the home nation."

Voiceover: "The Second World War was a killing blow to the British Empire, accelerating a chain of events that would see countries withdrawing from the Empire en-masse in some cases, at the cost of thousands of lives. In this four-part series, we will explore the fight for independence from colonial rule, by journeying through IWM’s newest exhibition: Emergency Exits. But first, in this episode, we need to understand the British Empire as a whole. How did it work? What did Britain gain from controlling so many countries? And why, after centuries, did it all come tumbling down?" Carl Warner, IWM curator: "Empires are deceptively simple concepts. Fundamentally, an empire is acquired to bring benefit to the nation that owns it. And some places are required because they guarantee that that benefit will continue because they're in key strategic locations. Although Empire is often presented as a much more complex sort of proposition, at its heart, it's about ensuring the benefits flow to the home nation." This is exactly how the British Empire operated. Each colony directly benefitted and enriched Britain, and British people. This usually came in the form of resources, with each region contributing different materials to sustain the empire. 

Historically, this was often at the expense of indigenous populations, who were regularly oppressed and abused. Despite Britain formally abolishing slavery in the early 1800s, local populations were still mistreated and exploited across the empire through to the 20th century. Indentured labourers worked in extremely harsh conditions for little to no pay, all the way up to the First World War. When that conflict began it created a whole new set of challenges for those living in colonised countries. 

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "The empire not only provided resources and soldiers, it carefully managed how it used those resources. And, crucially, it carefully managed how it used those people. So, the people of the empire were restricted to particular roles, often non-combat roles. 

This is a sealed pattern jacket. So the idea behind things like this is that they were made once. And then this would be the example that all of the manufacturers of these jackets would go back to, in order to make sure that their products were the same. And this is a sealed pattern for the South African Native Labour Corps, and the crucial thing about the roles that the guys who wore this performed was that they were support roles; fundamentally, the British Government didn't want black soldiers fighting white soldiers, white German soldiers, in Europe. And they also wanted to ensure that the roles that they had were carefully managed and based upon those ideas about what people in the colonies should do, rather than the sense of what they could do. So the South African Native Labour Corps was restricted to non-combat logistical roles; portering, fetching, carrying, digging and so on."

Voiceover: "Indian, African and Caribbean servicemen made an enormous contribution to the First World War, helping to secure Allied victory. Yet, after the conflict their contribution was widely forgotten. As the Commonwealth War Graves Commission concluded in 2021, up to 350,000 people who had served and died for Britain were not commemorated in the same way as their white comrades or possibly not commemorated at all."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "Imagery and the use of imagery is really, really important in wartime. So it's really carefully curated - the images that are put out by each side - because they wish to portray themselves in a certain light and their enemies in a very different light. This photograph was taken from a German Prisoner of War and shows black people chained, labour forces that have been recaptured by Germany - the power that controls them. 

These people are chained in ways that ordinarily would evoke feelings of, of horror, of disgust, memories of transatlantic slavery. If British soldiers were captured by German soldiers, they wouldn't have been chained by the neck. The types of treatment that these men are receiving here is extraordinarily different to the type of treatment that even enemy combatants would receive when made prisoners. And don't forget, these people are technically on the same side. 

And here, the person that goes through these images and decides which ones are going to be used to illustrate certain things about the enemy, has made a really interesting point and a very revealing point, because he says that we should be very careful that we're not suggesting that the enemy is doing anything that is necessarily improper by the treatment of these men, because, as the censor says, it's very likely that this is exactly how British forces would treat - and the quote here describing these men is - “native delinquents.”"

Voiceover: "At the end of the First World War, the question arose of what to do with the colonies of the defeated German and Ottoman empires. In the end, Britain gained control of several of these colonies through League of Nations mandates, which included control over Palestine, Mesopotamia and parts of former German colonies in Africa."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "So the addition of former German and Ottoman colonies into the British Empire means that in the 1920s, Britain's empire is huge. It controls around a quarter of the globe."

Voiceover: "But while these mandates were part of the British Empire, they did not operate in the same way as other British Colonies. The League of Nations oversaw the administration of these territories, with the goal of guiding them towards eventual self-governance. Other empire countries operated differently too. Dominions, such as Canada, Australia and New Zealand, were former colonies with their own governments and a high degree of autonomy, whilst still remaining under British sovereignty. 

Crown Colonies such as Kenya, Jamaica and Hong Kong were more directly controlled by Britain, with a British Governor appointed by the Crown, who directly ruled them. Protectorates were under British protection, but with varying levels of control, depending on the specific territory and its circumstances. 

A key turning point came in 1931, when Parliament passed the Statute of Westminster. This granted the Dominions full legislative independence from Britain, and formed a Commonwealth of Nations that were "autonomous communities within the British Empire”. The statute formalised the shift from Imperial rule to a more co-operative and voluntary structure for the founding members, which consisted of: Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, The Irish Free State and Newfoundland. Notably, this freedom was only granted to white-governed and established states. At this point, not a single government of a Dominion was made up of the people who lived in the country before European settlers arrived.

When the Second World War broke out, the Empire’s resources and supply lines became even more critical, as they were now directly supporting the war effort."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "This poster that we're standing in front of is a really great illustration of both the extent of the British Empire during the Second World War and immediately after, and also the complex ways in which it was governed. So, the thing that it really reveals is kind of one of the purposes, the main foundational purposes of empire, which is to extract resources from the countries that are part of it, and bring those resources or the wealth that comes from, trade in those resources back to the motherland. 

And that's particularly important during war because Britain relies upon the empire for all sorts of products, all sorts of natural resources, and of course, for labour and soldiers, sailors and airmen who come from these countries. But the crucial thing as we look at it is it talks about those principal products. And one of the things that empire, the British Empire does is that it frequently describes itself, or it is described as something that is, contributory kind of partnership so that there is equality on both sides. 

And of course, while many people in these countries were very proud of their links to Britain, very proud of their service to the empire, there remains this idea that fundamentally this is about extracting vital resources in order to continue the war effort."

Voiceover: "The resources of the British Empire allowed Britain to stay in the fight but access to these resources were quickly coming under threat. As Japan expanded its own empire during the Second World War, many British territories – along with their vital resources - fell under Japanese control. Hong Kong, Malaya and Burma were all rapidly occupied. But most costly of all was the fall of Singapore. Not only was it the largest surrender in British military history, but Britain also lost control of a vital strategic location and access to the crucial raw materials provided by Malaya."

Carl Warner: And the fall of Singapore is described by Winston Churchill as "The greatest capitulation in British history, a shattering moment for Britain and a great tragedy" because the thousands of British prisoners of war that had been taken, the thousands of civilian internees, are treated with appalling brutality by their Japanese captors. Many are murdered, thousands are tortured. And then following Japanese surrender in August 1945, the Union flags return. This particular flag was flown over the municipal buildings in Singapore in September 1945. 

An empire maintains its power, in part by conveying to people that it is uniquely good at governing. And as Lee Kuan Yew, the Prime Minister of Singapore, says when they see Britain removed from Singapore and the Japanese Empire come in suddenly that logic seemingly no longer applies. And that is a really powerful realisation."

Voiceover: "When the war ended, Britain regained control of its Southeast Asian territories. But whilst geographically the empire seemed to be whole once again, socially, politically and economically, it would never be the same."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "It cost a lot to fight the Second World War. Britain's economy is extremely damaged. One of the things that Britain then looks to do is to rebuild, reassert itself on the global stage."

Voiceover: "Post-war Britain was struggling. Significant war debt and damaged infrastructure meant economic recovery was far from immediate. Food was still being rationed and housing was in short supply. And so the issue of empire became less significant in relation to all of the problems people were experiencing at home. However, these territories would offer a way to ensure that Britain could rebuild - by once again exploiting the resources that they provided."

Carl Warner, IWM curator: "The interesting paradox at the heart of empire is, of course, they cost a lot to maintain. So, in order to bring those resources in order to guarantee that trade, it requires an outlay. Getting that balance right between how much Britain wants to spend on securing its empire and what it is getting from its empire, becomes a crucial question here in London."
